title: Specification for DNS over Transport Layer Security (TLS)
subtitle: How DNS queries get wrapped in TLS on port 853 so eavesdroppers cannot read them.
summary: DNS over TLS (DoT) sends ordinary DNS messages inside a TLS-protected TCP connection to port 853, so that anyone watching the network cannot read which names a client looks up. It keeps the existing DNS message format and its two-octet length prefix, and defines two usage profiles: opportunistic privacy, and out-of-band key-pinned authentication. It is meant for traffic between stub clients and recursive resolvers.

eli5.summary: Normally you whisper your question to the librarian in a crowded room, and everyone can hear it. DNS over TLS puts you and the librarian in a soundproof booth, so you ask the same question and nobody else hears.

tldr.problem: Classic DNS queries and answers travel in cleartext, so anyone on the network path can see which names a user looks up.
tldr.mechanism: The client opens a TCP connection to port 853, performs a TLS handshake, and then sends normal DNS messages, each with its two-octet length prefix, inside the encrypted session.
tldr.outcome: Eavesdroppers lose sight of the queries, while DNS itself is unchanged. It protects privacy only, not the correctness of answers, which is still DNSSEC's job.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The RFC starts from a plain observation: nearly all DNS queries are sent unencrypted, so an attacker with access to the network channel can eavesdrop, which reduces the privacy of the querier. DNSSEC does not help here. It provides response integrity by letting a resolver verify signed zones, and by intention it does not protect the privacy of requests or responses.

RFC 7858 therefore describes DNS over TLS on a well-known port, together with advice on keeping the cost of TCP and TLS low. It works between stub clients and recursive servers. It might work equally between recursive clients and authoritative servers, but that case is out of scope for the DPRIVE Working Group under its charter. Clients and servers are also expected to follow the TLS recommendations and security considerations of BCP 195 (RFC 7525).

DNS over TLS and DNSSEC are independent and fully compatible. Each solves a different problem, and using one does not remove the need for the other.
sections.eli5: When you ask a question out loud, everybody nearby can hear it, even if the answer is correct. This RFC is about making the question private, not about checking the answer.

sections.title: Starting a session on port 853
sections.content:
A DNS server that supports DNS over TLS MUST, by default, listen for and accept TCP connections on port 853. A client wanting privacy MUST connect to port 853 on the server. They may agree on another port, but it MUST NOT be port 53; it MAY come from the first-come, first-served range. The reason is to avoid complicating the choice between TLS and non-TLS, and to reduce the risk of downgrade attacks.

The first data exchanged on the connection MUST be the TLS handshake, following RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2) and the BCP 195 best practices. Port 853 is then reserved for encrypted traffic: clients and servers MUST NOT send or answer cleartext DNS on any port used for DNS over TLS, even after a failed handshake.

Clients SHOULD remember server IP addresses that do not support DNS over TLS (timeouts, refused connections, handshake failures) and not retry for a reasonable period, such as one hour per server.

An earlier draft upgraded a connection on port 53, STARTTLS-style, using a TLS OK bit in EDNS(0). The final text dropped that design and signals TLS by port alone.
sections.eli5: Instead of asking whether the librarian has a private booth, you just walk to the door marked for private chats. Nothing is ever said in that doorway except private talk.

sections.title: Handshake and messages
sections.content:
After the TCP connection is up, the client runs the TLS handshake and then authenticates the server if its profile requires it. The RFC proposes no new authentication ideas. Once negotiation completes, the connection is encrypted and protected from eavesdropping.

Inside the session, every request and response MUST use the two-octet length field from section 4.2.2 of RFC 1035, the same framing DNS already uses over TCP. Implementations SHOULD hand the length and the message to TCP together, for example in one write call, so they are likely to travel in one TCP segment.

Clients SHOULD pipeline several queries over one session rather than wait for each reply. Because pipelined answers can arrive out of order, clients MUST match each response to an outstanding query using the Message ID, and, if the response has a Question section, also QNAME, QCLASS and QTYPE.
sections.eli5: Once you are inside the booth, you can ask several questions in a row without waiting. Each answer carries a number so you know which question it belongs to.

sections.title: Reusing and closing connections
sections.content:
Setting up TCP and TLS is expensive, so clients and servers SHOULD NOT close the connection after each response. They SHOULD reuse it for later queries as long as resources allow, which means keeping idle connections open for a while. The RFC deliberately gives no specific timeout values. Successful TLS negotiation is taken to mean both sides are willing to keep idle connections, whatever the usual DNS-over-TCP timeouts say.

Both sides MUST still cope with the connection being closed by the other party. Servers MAY close at any time, perhaps under resource pressure, and clients MUST handle abrupt closes and be ready to reconnect and retry queries.

Reconnection can be sped up with TCP Fast Open (RFC 7413) and TLS session resumption (RFC 5077). Even with Fast Open, the TLS handshake must begin or resume immediately and no cleartext DNS may be exchanged. When closing, servers SHOULD use the TLS close-notify request to shift TCP TIME-WAIT state to the client. Further guidance is in RFC 7766.
sections.eli5: Walking in and out of the booth for every question would be slow. It is better to stay inside and keep asking, though either of you may leave whenever you need to.

sections.title: Usage profiles
sections.content:
The RFC defines two profiles that trade convenience for assurance.

In the opportunistic privacy profile, the client wants privacy when possible but does not require it. It might learn of a TLS-capable resolver from an untrusted source, for instance the DHCP DNS server option (RFC 3646), and then try port 853, with or without validating the resolver. This maximizes availability and performance, but it only provides privacy when no active on-path attacker is present.

In the out-of-band key-pinned profile, the client has a trust relationship with the server, such as an enterprise resolver or a public resolver it was configured for, and holds a set of SPKI fingerprint pins obtained out of band. After the handshake it computes fingerprints for the public keys in the server's certificate chain (or the raw public key) and, if none matches a pin, MUST treat the failure as non-recoverable. Administrators SHOULD deploy a backup pin. Implementations MUST support a SHA-256 fingerprint of the DER-encoded SPKI, represented as a base64 string.

The RFC expected a further document to define more authentication methods; that became RFC 8310.
sections.eli5: One way is to talk to whichever helper you find, and hope nobody swapped places with them. The stricter way is to have a photo of the right helper beforehand and refuse to talk unless the face matches.

sections.title: Performance considerations
sections.content:
DNS over TLS costs more than plain UDP DNS, and the RFC lists where. Latency: TCP adds one round trip over UDP, which TCP Fast Open can remove when information from earlier connections exists, and the TLS handshake adds two more round trips. Keepalive, out-of-order processing, TLS session resumption and TLS False Start can amortize this. State: connections need memory in both kernel and application, which matters on servers with many clients; shorter timeouts reduce concurrent connections, and servers can close connections when limits are hit. Processing: encryption means slightly higher CPU, and servers can refuse new clients when over their limits.

To limit connections, clients SHOULD minimize creating new TCP connections. A local DNS request aggregator, a kind of forwarder, can funnel a whole machine through one DNS-over-TLS connection. The RFC says a full performance evaluation is out of its scope.
sections.eli5: A private booth takes a little time to enter and a little effort to keep up, so you enter once and stay, instead of coming and going.

sections.title: Security considerations and limits
sections.content:
DNS over TLS addresses the risk of eavesdropping on DNS messages and nothing more. The RFC names residual risks. General TLS attacks such as person-in-the-middle and protocol downgrade still apply, and clients that remember which servers support TLS can detect downgrades. For a server with no history, a client may try another server, continue without TLS, or refuse to forward the query, depending on its profile.

Middleboxes can interfere with DNS, though a designated port should avoid that. Any DNS interaction in the clear can be modified by an on-path attacker, so clients MAY discard cached information about server capabilities that was advertised in cleartext.

The RFC does not itself resist traffic analysis. Even encrypted, message timings and sizes can leak details. Padding (RFC 7830) may help but simple padding alone might not suffice.
sections.eli5: The booth hides what you say, but someone outside might still tell how long you talked or how loud the question was. And it does not prove the librarian is telling the truth.

sections.title: IANA port assignment
sections.content:
IANA added an entry to the Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry in the System range, through the early allocation process. The registry for that range requires IETF Review or IESG Approval. The same port number was also reserved over UDP for the proposed DNS-over-DTLS protocol.

The registration reads: service name domain-s, port number 853, transport TCP/UDP, assignee IESG, contact IETF Chair, description "DNS query-response protocol run over TLS/DTLS", reference this document.

The RFC's Design Evolution section explains why a dedicated port beat the upgrade approach. A port avoids the extra round trip of a dummy query, avoids making downgrade attacks indistinguishable from broken middleboxes, and lets both TLS and DTLS share one well-known port. The cost is a new port that firewalls may block.
sections.eli5: The internet keeps a phone book of door numbers. Door 853 was set aside, so everyone knows where the private booth is.

items.title: Latency
items.text: One extra round trip for TCP, two more for the TLS handshake; Fast Open, resumption and reuse reduce them.

items.title: State
items.text: Open connections need kernel and application memory on the server.

items.title: Processing
items.text: Encryption uses slightly more CPU than plain DNS.

items.title: Connections
items.text: Reuse one session, or aggregate through a local forwarder.

today: DNS over TLS is widely supported. Public resolvers such as Cloudflare (1.1.1.1), Google Public DNS and Quad9 accept it on port 853, and Android's "Private DNS" setting uses it. Many resolver and stub implementations, including Unbound, BIND, Knot Resolver and systemd-resolved, support it. RFC 8310 added more authentication methods and updated this document, and DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484) arrived as an alternative that shares port 443 with web traffic.

implementations.name: Unbound
implementations.note: Supports DNS over TLS both as a client toward upstream resolvers and as a server.

implementations.name: Stubby / getdns
implementations.note: A local stub resolver built to use DNS over TLS.

implementations.name: systemd-resolved
implementations.note: Supports an opportunistic and strict DNS-over-TLS mode.

implementations.name: Android Private DNS
implementations.note: Uses DNS over TLS on port 853.
